folded.subject: Scheme is
folded.object: of the smallest

spans.text: It is interesting that among all the programming languages in the world, Scheme is one of the smallest, while Common Lisp is one of the largest.

folded.id: scheme is|the|only dialect of lisp besides common lisp that is currently flourishing
folded.subject: Scheme is
folded.object: only dialect of Lisp besides Common Lisp that is currently flourishing

spans.text: Scheme is the only dialect of Lisp besides Common Lisp that is currently flourishing.

folded.id: scheme manual|is|only 45 pages (only 38 if you omit the example
folded.subject: Scheme manual
folded.object: only 45 pages (only 38 if you omit the example

spans.text: The Scheme manual is only 45 pages (only 38 if you omit the example, bibliography, and index), while *Common Lisp the Language*, 2d edition, is 1029 pages.

folded.id: scheme uses|the|same name space for functions and variables (and everything else)
folded.subject: Scheme uses
folded.object: same name space for functions and variables (and everything else)

spans.text: Scheme uses the same name space for functions and variables (and everything else).
Scheme evaluates the function part of a function call in exactly the same way as the arguments.

folded.id: scheme|has|fewer built-in functions and special forms
folded.subject: Scheme
folded.object: fewer built-in functions and special forms

spans.text: Scheme has fewer built-in functions and special forms.
Scheme has no special variables, only lexical variables.
Scheme has no special forms for looping; instead it asks the user to use recursion and promises to implement the recursion efficiently.

folded.id: scheme|has|no `block`
folded.subject: Scheme
folded.object: no `block`

spans.text: Scheme has no `block`, `return`, `go`, or `throw`; a single function `(call/cc)` replaces all of these (and does much more).

folded.id: scheme|has|no packages
folded.subject: Scheme
folded.object: no packages

spans.text: Scheme has no packages.

folded.id: scheme|has|some spelling conventions that are different from common lisp
folded.subject: Scheme
folded.object: some spelling conventions that are different from Common Lisp

spans.text: However, Scheme has some spelling conventions that are different from Common Lisp.

folded.id: scheme|tries|to give a minimal set of very powerful features that can be used to implement the others
folded.subject: Scheme
folded.object: to give a minimal set of very powerful features that can be used to implement the others

spans.text: Where Common Lisp tries to standardize all the important features that are in current use by Lisp programmers, Scheme tries to give a minimal set of very powerful features that can be used to implement the others.

folded.id: so|the|predicate is `pair?`
folded.subject: so
folded.object: predicate is `pair?`

spans.text: Despite the fact that Scheme has `cons`, it calls the result a `pair` rather than a cons cell, so the predicate is `pair?`, not `consp`.

folded.id: this convention|is|in spoken language: is `equal?` pronounced "equal-question-mark" or "equal-q" or perhaps equal
folded.subject: this convention
folded.object: in spoken language: is `equal?` pronounced "equal-question-mark" or "equal-q" or perhaps equal

spans.text: This makes predicates more obvious and eliminates the complicated conventions for adding a hyphen before the `p`.[1](#fn22-1) The only problem with this convention is in spoken language: is `equal?` pronounced "equal-question-mark" or "equal-q" or perhaps equal, with rising intonation?

folded.subject: translation of
folded.object: program into some other language-usually a languag

spans.text: A compiler takes a program as input and produces as output a translation of that program into some other language-usually a languag

folded.subject: understanding how
folded.object: interpreter works can give you a better appreciation of how Lisp works

spans.text: While it is not likely that you would use this interpreter for any serious programming, understanding how the interpreter works can give you a better appreciation of how Lisp works, and thus make you a better programmer.

folded.id: which|is|as in common lisp
folded.subject: which
folded.object: as in Common Lisp

spans.text: The five main special forms in Scheme are `quote` and `if`, which are just as in Common Lisp; `begin` and `set!`, which are just different spellings for `progn` and `setq`; and `lambda`, which is as in Common Lisp, except that it doesn't require a `#'` before it.

folded.subject: While it
folded.object: not likely that you would use this interpreter for any serious programming

spans.text: While it is not likely that you would use this interpreter for any serious programming, understanding how the interpreter works can give you a better appreciation of how Lisp works, and thus make you a better programmer.
